source.title: PonderLM-2: Pretraining LLM with Latent Thoughts in Continuous Space
source.authors: Bo-Yi Zeng; He Li; Shi-Xiang Song; Yixuan Wang; Zi-Tong Wang; Ziwei He; Xinbing Wang; Zhou-Han Lin

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation, garbling, or wrong-document issue.
record.tranche_reason: Reports language-model loss scaling results in the new setting of latent-thought pretraining, but does not reproduce or fit the original scaling-law analyses.
record.gate_note: The study reports loss comparisons across model sizes and training-token budgets. It does not report fitted power-law exponents, prediction errors from small-run fits, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Downstream-task results and comparisons among latent-thought methods are not rows for the claim versions because they do not measure the scaling-law properties named there.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. Its scaling curves (Fig. 1, Fig. 10) are used to show that PonderLM-2 is more parameter- and data-efficient than vanilla baselines. In Fig. 10 the vanilla models get a fitted curve, and the method's gain is read off it as an equivalent parameter×token multiplier (2.48x, 2.46x). No exponents, fit quality or extrapolation test are reported. The vanilla sweep spans only 405M–1.4B parameters (about 12x in parameter×tokens). The Pythia curves are the official suite's existing results. So the study relies on scaling behaviour as a yardstick and reports only its own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that pretraining with latent thoughts lets a model outperform a standard model with twice the parameters at equal inference cost. They also find it beats looped, pause-token and PonderLM baselines even when those use more inference compute, and that chaining more latent thoughts consistently improves performance. They frame this as a new dimension for scaling. They make no claims about power-law form or compute-optimal allocation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a distinct latent-thought pretraining method with Jacobi-iteration training; it does not fit the original scaling-law models or estimate compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that increasing latent-thought chain length improves loss and downstream scores, and that results depend on the number of Jacobi iterations; these are method ablations, not sensitivity tests of scaling-law fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Chaining more latent thoughts per token lowers loss monotonically. Pile PPL goes 12.4, 11.2, 10.7, 10.4 for K=0,1,3,5 on LLaMA-410M, 6B tokens (Table 8; also Fig. 7 on Pythia-70m).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss improves with the number of latent-thought steps per token during pretraining (a per-token compute scaling axis).

record.problems: The scaling evidence is reported as performance comparisons and curves without numerical loss values or power-law fits; the reported sweep does not cover several orders of magnitude in model size.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted downstream-task tables, continual-pretraining comparisons, and latent-thought-count ablations because they do not test the scaling-law properties named by the versions.

untested.parts: No fitted exponents or power-law form are reported. The vanilla sweep covers about 1 order of magnitude. Pythia curves are reused official results.
Token budgets follow the Chinchilla ratio by design; the compute-optimal split is not measured.
No comparison of model shapes at fixed parameter count.
Text only. Continual pretraining is reported without scaling fits.
Downstream accuracies are reported, but not tested as predictable from scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests classification is wrong: all four rows compare the study's own method with baselines. Training FLOPs for the method are about 8x vanilla per token, so the 'fewer tokens/params' comparisons are not compute-matched. Figure 10's fitted vanilla curves could inform V1 only if the fit parameters were given, and they are not.

versions.untested_parts: The reported comparisons do not establish a power-law functional form, fitted exponents, or behavior over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of a substantially larger run.
No loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation is measured as a function of training compute.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies text pretraining and text continual pretraining, but does not test whether power laws hold in other modalities or regimes.
Downstream tasks are evaluated, but the study does not test predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, nor test whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: PonderLM-2-Pythia-1.26B
rows.operation_detail: Compared language-model loss across parameter counts in the Pythia and PonderLM-2-Pythia scaling curves.
rows.baseline: Official Pythia-2.8B; its loss value is not stated in text.
rows.value: Matches the performance of official Pythia-2.8B with 55% fewer parameters.
rows.note: The paper reports a matched-performance comparison, not a power-law fit or numerical loss.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method with official Pythia (a matched-performance claim). It is not a test of power-law loss scaling and should not be a V1 row.

rows.subject: PonderLM-2-Pythia-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Compared language-model loss across training-token budgets in the Pythia and PonderLM-2-Pythia scaling curves.
rows.baseline: Official Pythia-1.4B; its loss value is not stated in text.
rows.value: Converges to the official version’s final performance using 62% less training data.
rows.note: The comparison states a data-efficiency result but gives neither the exact token count at the match nor a power-law fit.
rows.check: A data-efficiency comparison of the study's own method against Pythia-1.4B. It does not measure how loss scales with tokens.

rows.subject: PonderLM-2-GPT-834M
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across model sizes and training-token budgets against vanilla GPT models.

conditions.value: 7B, 15B, and 26B across the reported size sweep

rows.baseline: Vanilla GPT counterpart; exact loss not stated in text.
rows.value: Validation loss comparable to the vanilla counterpart trained with approximately 2.48x the parameter-token product.
rows.note: The text reports the comparison, but not a power-law fit or numerical loss values.
rows.check: The 2.48x multiplier is the method's gain read against a fitted vanilla GPT curve, so it uses a scaling fit as a tool. No fit parameters or fit quality are reported; this is not a test of V1.
